## The three mechanisms and which format versions support them

The spec's "Delete Formats" section (spec.md L1356–1471) defines three encodings:

| Mechanism | V1 | V2 | V3 | V4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Position delete files** (row deleted by `file_path + pos`) | ✗ | ✓ | deprecated — must not write new ones; existing valid | same as V3 (no new) |
| **Equality delete files** (row deleted by column value match) | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | prohibited — must not add new; existing still applied |
| **Deletion vectors** (bitmap of positions) | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |

The authoritative version statement is spec.md L109–116:

> "Position deletes -- Mark a row deleted by data file path and the row position … encoded in a _position delete file_ (V2) or _deletion vector_ (V3 or above). Equality deletes -- Mark a row deleted by one or more column values … (may be created in v2 and v3 tables only)."

And the hard constraints in the delete-formats intro (spec.md L1357–1359):

> "Position delete files must not be added to v3 tables, but existing position delete files are valid. Equality delete files must not be added to v4 tables, but existing equality delete files are valid."

- **Position delete files** store `file_path` (field id 2147483546), `pos` (2147483545), and optionally the deleted `row` (2147483544); rows must be sorted by `file_path` then `pos` (spec.md L1391–1417). They're deprecated in v3 (spec.md L1393–1394) and replaced by DVs.
- **Equality delete files** store a subset of table columns; the matching columns are `equality_ids` in the delete file's metadata. Semantics: multiple columns are an AND of equality predicates, and a `null` delete-column value matches `col IS NULL` (spec.md L1418–1460).
- **Deletion vectors** encode deleted positions as a bitmap (Roaring, keyed by high 32 bits), stored as the `deletion-vector-v1` blob in Puffin files, referenced by `file_path` + `content_offset` + `content_size_in_bytes` (spec.md L1375–1390). "At most one deletion vector is allowed per data file in a snapshot" and "if a DV is written for a data file, it must replace all previously written position delete files" (spec.md L1388–1390).

All three are tracked in manifest files (data `content` field = 0/1/2 at spec.md L713–719, plus `referenced_data_file`, `content_offset`, `content_size_in_bytes`, `equality_ids` at L726, 735–738). Unlike data files, delete files and DVs live in **delete manifests** (`content: 1`, spec.md L664, L1023).

## When a reader applies them

The spec's `Scan Planning` rules (spec.md L1071–1097) define exactly when each applies to a given data file:

- **Deletion vector** applies when: data file `file_path` == DV's `referenced_data_file`; data file's data sequence number ≤ DV's data sequence number; partitions equal (spec.md L1075–1078).
- **Position delete file** applies when: same file-path condition (via `referenced_data_file` if set); data `seq ≤ delete seq`; partitions equal; **and there is no DV that must be applied to the file** (spec.md L1079–1083). That last clause is the "DV supersedes position deletes" rule.
- **Equality delete file** applies when: data `seq < delete seq` (**strictly less**); and partitions equal **or** the delete is in an unpartitioned spec (global) (spec.md L1084–1087).
- General rule: "deletes are applied only to data files that are older and in the same partition" (spec.md L1088), with two exceptions — global equality deletes from unpartitioned specs, and position deletes applying to files from the same commit when seq numbers are equal (spec.md L1088–1097).

The reader-side implementation is `DeleteFileIndex` (DeleteFileIndex.java:61–64: "An index of DeleteFiles by sequence number"). In a scan, the builder reads the delete manifests once (in parallel), prunes them with scan filters, and buckets each delete file by content type during `build()` (DeleteFileIndex.java:541–556): DVs → `dvByPath`; other position deletes → `posDeletesByPath`/`posDeletesByPartition`; equality deletes → global or per-partition (DeleteFileIndex.java:604–611, keyed on `spec.isUnpartitioned()`).

Then for each data file, `forDataFile(long sequenceNumber, DataFile file)` (DeleteFileIndex.java:158) does the lookup (lines 163–173), exactly mirroring the spec rules:

```java
DeleteFile[] global     = findGlobalDeletes(sequenceNumber, file);     // line 163
DeleteFile[] eqPartition= findEqPartitionDeletes(sequenceNumber, file);// line 164
DeleteFile dv           = findDV(sequenceNumber, file);                // line 165
if (dv != null && global == null && eqPartition == null) { return {dv}; }
else if (dv != null) { return concat(global, eqPartition, {dv}); }    // DV present → skip pos deletes
else { /* posPartition + posPath */ }                                  // lines 171-173
```

- **Sequence number** filtering is a binary search on sorted delete seq numbers (`findStartIndex`, DeleteFileIndex.java:686–706; `PositionDeletes.filter`, lines 726–742) selecting deletes with seq ≥ data seq. For equality deletes, files are sorted by `applySequenceNumber`, which is `wrapped.dataSequenceNumber() - 1` (DeleteFileIndex.java:881) — that −1 materializes the spec's **strict** `<` rule for equality deletes.
- **Partition matching**: equality/path/partition deletes looked up by `(specId, partition)` or path (lines 177–212); every path/DV hit is re-validated against the data file's spec + partition tuple (`validatePartitionMatch`, lines 234–253, failing on "metadata is corrupted"). The DV also asserts `dv.dataSequenceNumber() >= seq` (lines 221–225).
- **Per-file bound pruning for equality deletes**: `EqualityDeletes.filter` calls `canContainEqDeletesForFile` (DeleteFileIndex.java:258–300), which skips a delete whose equality-column [lower, upper] doesn't overlap the data file's bounds (`rangesOverlap`, lines 318–329) or whose null counts prove no match — the reader-side version of "Column metrics can be used to determine whether a delete file's rows overlap the contents of a data file" (spec.md L115).
- **DV fast path**: only one DV per data file can exist (enforced at index build, DeleteFileIndex.java:570–573), and its presence short-circuits position-delete search (lines 165–170) — spec's "readers can safely ignore matching position delete files" (spec.md L1388–1389).

Finally, the data rows that survive are produced by removing the marked positions (DVs/position deletes) or by anti-joining against equality-delete values, per the format's encoding — and position/equality delete files can optionally carry the deleted row values for reconstructing change streams (spec.md L1402–1417, L1420).

## What compaction does with them

Compaction is a **`REPLACE`** operation implemented by `BaseRewriteFiles` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:28–29, `operation()` returns `DataOperations.REPLACE`).

The core API is `rewriteFiles(dataFilesToReplace, deleteFilesToReplace, dataFilesToAdd, deleteFilesToAdd)` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:92–119): the compacted, delete-free **rewritten** data files go in as `addFile(...)` (lines 67–74) and the old files come out as `deleteFile(...)` (lines 48–56) — all in one snapshot commit (via `MergingSnapshotProducer`/`SnapshotProducer`).

**What happens to each delete type:**

1. **Position deletes / DVs**: compaction reads the surviving rows (applying delete files via `DeleteFileIndex`), writes new data files that physically exclude the deleted rows, and typically also removes the now-redundant delete files in the same rewrite — `deleteFile(DeleteFile)` at BaseRewriteFiles.java:55–56, and `deleteFilesToReplace` at lines 107–108. The new data files get a **new data sequence number** (via `dataSequenceNumber(long)`, BaseRewriteFiles.java:79–81, or the rewrite's current snapshot seq), so any *old* position delete whose seq is now less than the new file's seq no longer applies per the `seq ≤ delete seq` rule (spec.md L1079–1083) — the ownership of the delete problem shifts from delete files to rewritten files.

2. **Equality deletes**: the spec allows a "replace" to keep or drop equality delete files (spec.md L82–83: rewrite applies "if all of the rewritten files are still in the table"). Because equality deletes apply by **value** with a strict `<` rule, a rewritten file that keeps its original (older) data sequence number remains subject to equality deletes added later at higher sequence numbers.

**The concurrency safety check** is the important part — compaction must not delete rows that another writer just deleted. `BaseRewriteFiles.validate` calls `validateNoNewDeletesForDataFiles(base, startingSnapshotId, replacedDataFiles, parent)` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:135–140), whose javadoc says it all: "Validates that no new delete files that must be applied to the given data files have been added to the table since a starting snapshot" (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:483–490). Concretely (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:519–544):

```java
deleteFiles = deletes.forDataFile(startingSequenceNumber, dataFile);
if (ignoreEqualityDeletes) {
  ValidationException.check(!containsPositionDeletes(deleteFiles),
      "Cannot commit, found new position delete for replaced data file: %s", dataFile);
  ...
```

- A new **position** delete (or DV) targeting a replaced data file ⇒ **commit fails** (the deleted rows can't be recovered).
- New **equality** deletes can be ignored *only* when "the added data files have the same sequence number as the replaced data files, equality deletes added at a higher sequence number are still effective against the added data files, so there is no risk of commit conflict between RewriteFiles and RowDelta" (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:501–510) — i.e. the rewritten file inherits the delete's effective scope.

There are also structural invariants in `validateReplacedAndAddedFiles` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:144–153): you can't add files without deleting any, and delete-file rewrites must be paired (`deletesDeleteFiles() || !addsDeleteFiles()`).

**After** compaction, the old (replaced) data files are no longer referenced by any live snapshot, so the next snapshot **expiration** deletes them physically — the reachable-manifest-subtraction in `ReachableFileCleanup.findFilesToDelete` removes any path still listed in a current manifest via `filesToDelete::remove` (ReachableFileCleanup.java:216–217), keeping only truly unreachable files, and the incremental strategy only reverts/deletes files whose status is backed by expired, non-ancestor snapshots (IncrementalFileCleanup.java:302–303, 326). Compaction-plus-expiration is thus the mechanism by which position/equality deletes and DVs are eventually "materialized away" — Iceberg never rewrites in place, it rewrites-and-expires.

## One-line summary

- **Position deletes** (V2+, deprecated V3+) mark `(file, row_pos)` pairs in delete files; **equality deletes** (V2, V3; prohibited V4) mark rows by column values via `equality_ids`; **deletion vectors** (V3+) are per-file position bitmaps stored in Puffin, superseding position delete files.
- A **reader** applies a delete file only when the sequence-number ordering (≤ for position/DV, strictly < for equality), the partition/spec match, and (for DVs/paths) file identity all hold, and only when column bounds suggest overlap — computed per data file via `DeleteFileIndex` (DeleteFileIndex.java:158–173, 686–881) against the spec's scan-planning rules (spec.md L1071–1097).
- **Compaction** reads the delete-filtered rows, writes new data files at a fresh sequence number, and atomically removes the old data files (+ optionally the delete files) in a `REPLACE` commit (BaseRewriteFiles.java:92–119), guarded by `validateNoNewDeletesForDataFiles` so it never commits over a concurrent delete of the same rows (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:475–544); the superseded files are later garbage-collected by snapshot expiration's reachability check (ReachableFileCleanup.java:216–217).

> "Position delete files must not be added to v3 tables, but existing position delete files are valid. Equality delete files must not be added to v4 tables, but existing equality delete files are valid."

- **Position delete files** store `file_path` (field id 2147483546), `pos` (2147483545), and optionally the deleted `row` (2147483544); rows must be sorted by `file_path` then `pos` (spec.md L1391–1417). They're deprecated in v3 (spec.md L1393–1394) and replaced by DVs.
- **Equality delete files** store a subset of table columns; the matching columns are `equality_ids` in the delete file's metadata. Semantics: multiple columns are an AND of equality predicates, and a `null` delete-column value matches `col IS NULL` (spec.md L1418–1460).
- **Deletion vectors** encode deleted positions as a bitmap (Roaring, keyed by high 32 bits), stored as the `deletion-vector-v1` blob in Puffin files, referenced by `file_path` + `content_offset` + `content_size_in_bytes` (spec.md L1375–1390). "At most one deletion vector is allowed per data file in a snapshot" and "if a DV is written for a data file, it must replace all previously written position delete files" (spec.md L1388–1390).

All three are tracked in manifest files (data `content` field = 0/1/2 at spec.md L713–719, plus `referenced_data_file`, `content_offset`, `content_size_in_bytes`, `equality_ids` at L726, 735–738). Unlike data files, delete files and DVs live in **delete manifests** (`content: 1`, spec.md L664, L1023).

## When a reader applies them

The spec's `Scan Planning` rules (spec.md L1071–1097) define exactly when each applies to a given data file:

- **Deletion vector** applies when: data file `file_path` == DV's `referenced_data_file`; data file's data sequence number ≤ DV's data sequence number; partitions equal (spec.md L1075–1078).
- **Position delete file** applies when: same file-path condition (via `referenced_data_file` if set); data `seq ≤ delete seq`; partitions equal; **and there is no DV that must be applied to the file** (spec.md L1079–1083). That last clause is the "DV supersedes position deletes" rule.
- **Equality delete file** applies when: data `seq < delete seq` (**strictly less**); and partitions equal **or** the delete is in an unpartitioned spec (global) (spec.md L1084–1087).
- General rule: "deletes are applied only to data files that are older and in the same partition" (spec.md L1088), with two exceptions — global equality deletes from unpartitioned specs, and position deletes applying to files from the same commit when seq numbers are equal (spec.md L1088–1097).

The reader-side implementation is `DeleteFileIndex` (DeleteFileIndex.java:61–64: "An index of DeleteFiles by sequence number"). In a scan, the builder reads the delete manifests once (in parallel), prunes them with scan filters, and buckets each delete file by content type during `build()` (DeleteFileIndex.java:541–556): DVs → `dvByPath`; other position deletes → `posDeletesByPath`/`posDeletesByPartition`; equality deletes → global or per-partition (DeleteFileIndex.java:604–611, keyed on `spec.isUnpartitioned()`).

Then for each data file, `forDataFile(long sequenceNumber, DataFile file)` (DeleteFileIndex.java:158) does the lookup (lines 163–173), exactly mirroring the spec rules:

```java
DeleteFile[] global     = findGlobalDeletes(sequenceNumber, file);     // line 163
DeleteFile[] eqPartition= findEqPartitionDeletes(sequenceNumber, file);// line 164
DeleteFile dv           = findDV(sequenceNumber, file);                // line 165
if (dv != null && global == null && eqPartition == null) { return {dv}; }
else if (dv != null) { return concat(global, eqPartition, {dv}); }    // DV present → skip pos deletes
else { /* posPartition + posPath */ }                                  // lines 171-173
```

- **Sequence number** filtering is a binary search on sorted delete seq numbers (`findStartIndex`, DeleteFileIndex.java:686–706; `PositionDeletes.filter`, lines 726–742) selecting deletes with seq ≥ data seq. For equality deletes, files are sorted by `applySequenceNumber`, which is `wrapped.dataSequenceNumber() - 1` (DeleteFileIndex.java:881) — that −1 materializes the spec's **strict** `<` rule for equality deletes.
- **Partition matching**: equality/path/partition deletes looked up by `(specId, partition)` or path (lines 177–212); every path/DV hit is re-validated against the data file's spec + partition tuple (`validatePartitionMatch`, lines 234–253, failing on "metadata is corrupted"). The DV also asserts `dv.dataSequenceNumber() >= seq` (lines 221–225).
- **Per-file bound pruning for equality deletes**: `EqualityDeletes.filter` calls `canContainEqDeletesForFile` (DeleteFileIndex.java:258–300), which skips a delete whose equality-column [lower, upper] doesn't overlap the data file's bounds (`rangesOverlap`, lines 318–329) or whose null counts prove no match — the reader-side version of "Column metrics can be used to determine whether a delete file's rows overlap the contents of a data file" (spec.md L115).
- **DV fast path**: only one DV per data file can exist (enforced at index build, DeleteFileIndex.java:570–573), and its presence short-circuits position-delete search (lines 165–170) — spec's "readers can safely ignore matching position delete files" (spec.md L1388–1389).

Finally, the data rows that survive are produced by removing the marked positions (DVs/position deletes) or by anti-joining against equality-delete values, per the format's encoding — and position/equality delete files can optionally carry the deleted row values for reconstructing change streams (spec.md L1402–1417, L1420).

## What compaction does with them

Compaction is a **`REPLACE`** operation implemented by `BaseRewriteFiles` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:28–29, `operation()` returns `DataOperations.REPLACE`).

The core API is `rewriteFiles(dataFilesToReplace, deleteFilesToReplace, dataFilesToAdd, deleteFilesToAdd)` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:92–119): the compacted, delete-free **rewritten** data files go in as `addFile(...)` (lines 67–74) and the old files come out as `deleteFile(...)` (lines 48–56) — all in one snapshot commit (via `MergingSnapshotProducer`/`SnapshotProducer`).

**What happens to each delete type:**

1. **Position deletes / DVs**: compaction reads the surviving rows (applying delete files via `DeleteFileIndex`), writes new data files that physically exclude the deleted rows, and typically also removes the now-redundant delete files in the same rewrite — `deleteFile(DeleteFile)` at BaseRewriteFiles.java:55–56, and `deleteFilesToReplace` at lines 107–108. The new data files get a **new data sequence number** (via `dataSequenceNumber(long)`, BaseRewriteFiles.java:79–81, or the rewrite's current snapshot seq), so any *old* position delete whose seq is now less than the new file's seq no longer applies per the `seq ≤ delete seq` rule (spec.md L1079–1083) — the ownership of the delete problem shifts from delete files to rewritten files.

2. **Equality deletes**: the spec allows a "replace" to keep or drop equality delete files (spec.md L82–83: rewrite applies "if all of the rewritten files are still in the table"). Because equality deletes apply by **value** with a strict `<` rule, a rewritten file that keeps its original (older) data sequence number remains subject to equality deletes added later at higher sequence numbers.

**The concurrency safety check** is the important part — compaction must not delete rows that another writer just deleted. `BaseRewriteFiles.validate` calls `validateNoNewDeletesForDataFiles(base, startingSnapshotId, replacedDataFiles, parent)` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:135–140), whose javadoc says it all: "Validates that no new delete files that must be applied to the given data files have been added to the table since a starting snapshot" (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:483–490). Concretely (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:519–544):

```java
deleteFiles = deletes.forDataFile(startingSequenceNumber, dataFile);
if (ignoreEqualityDeletes) {
  ValidationException.check(!containsPositionDeletes(deleteFiles),
      "Cannot commit, found new position delete for replaced data file: %s", dataFile);
  ...
```

- A new **position** delete (or DV) targeting a replaced data file ⇒ **commit fails** (the deleted rows can't be recovered).
- New **equality** deletes can be ignored *only* when "the added data files have the same sequence number as the replaced data files, equality deletes added at a higher sequence number are still effective against the added data files, so there is no risk of commit conflict between RewriteFiles and RowDelta" (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:501–510) — i.e. the rewritten file inherits the delete's effective scope.

There are also structural invariants in `validateReplacedAndAddedFiles` (BaseRewriteFiles.java:144–153): you can't add files without deleting any, and delete-file rewrites must be paired (`deletesDeleteFiles() || !addsDeleteFiles()`).

**After** compaction, the old (replaced) data files are no longer referenced by any live snapshot, so the next snapshot **expiration** deletes them physically — the reachable-manifest-subtraction in `ReachableFileCleanup.findFilesToDelete` removes any path still listed in a current manifest via `filesToDelete::remove` (ReachableFileCleanup.java:216–217), keeping only truly unreachable files, and the incremental strategy only reverts/deletes files whose status is backed by expired, non-ancestor snapshots (IncrementalFileCleanup.java:302–303, 326). Compaction-plus-expiration is thus the mechanism by which position/equality deletes and DVs are eventually "materialized away" — Iceberg never rewrites in place, it rewrites-and-expires.

## One-line summary

- **Position deletes** (V2+, deprecated V3+) mark `(file, row_pos)` pairs in delete files; **equality deletes** (V2, V3; prohibited V4) mark rows by column values via `equality_ids`; **deletion vectors** (V3+) are per-file position bitmaps stored in Puffin, superseding position delete files.
- A **reader** applies a delete file only when the sequence-number ordering (≤ for position/DV, strictly < for equality), the partition/spec match, and (for DVs/paths) file identity all hold, and only when column bounds suggest overlap — computed per data file via `DeleteFileIndex` (DeleteFileIndex.java:158–173, 686–881) against the spec's scan-planning rules (spec.md L1071–1097).
- **Compaction** reads the delete-filtered rows, writes new data files at a fresh sequence number, and atomically removes the old data files (+ optionally the delete files) in a `REPLACE` commit (BaseRewriteFiles.java:92–119), guarded by `validateNoNewDeletesForDataFiles` so it never commits over a concurrent delete of the same rows (MergingSnapshotProducer.java:475–544); the superseded files are later garbage-collected by snapshot expiration's reachability check (ReachableFileCleanup.java:216–217).
